options: (1) and (2) only
(1) and (3) only
(2) and (3) only
questions.explanation: Iron and steel production is capital-intensive rather than labour-intensive, so cheap labour is not a sufficient reason for the plant to stay in China. Agglomeration of heavy industries and upgraded production facilities are both genuine reasons, so (1) and (2) only is correct.

Cheese making is an example because milk is perishable and bulky, so it is processed close to where the milk is produced. Bread making uses flour that can be transported easily, and car manufacturing and newspaper printing are not raw material activities at all.

(1) and (3) only
(2) and (3) only

options: southward migration of biomes in the Southern Hemisphere
intensified coral bleaching in the polar region
more frequent extreme rainfall in Hong Kong
fewer forest fires in the Amazon rainforest
questions.explanation: Climate change shifts the climatic zones that support each biome, so biomes migrate towards the poles - southward in the Southern Hemisphere. Coral bleaching is a problem in warm tropical water, not the polar region; extreme rainfall in Hong Kong is a weather consequence rather than an ecological one; and the Amazon rainforest faces MORE forest fires, not fewer.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes Earth’s three main layers and their compositions?
options: The crust is solid, the mantle is semi-solid, and the core consists mainly of iron and nickel.
The crust is semi-solid, the mantle is solid, and the core consists mainly of iron and nickel.
The crust is solid, the mantle is molten, and the core consists mainly of iron and nickel.
The crust is solid, the mantle is semi-solid, and the core consists mainly of silicate rock.
questions.explanation: The solid crust overlies the semi-solid mantle, while the central core contains iron and nickel. B is incorrect because the crust, not the mantle, is the solid outermost layer.

questions.stem: Why is the weak asthenosphere important for plate movement?
options: Plates move over it, while rising magma within it spreads and pushes plates apart at ridges.
It forms a rigid outer shell that locks plates to the mantle and prevents their movement.
Its greater density makes plates sink into it and pull the ocean floor downwards.
It creates new crust at divergent boundaries but has no role in carrying the plates.
questions.explanation: Plates can move over the weak asthenosphere, where rising magma spreads and pushes plates apart at mid-ocean ridges. B confuses the weak asthenosphere with the rigid lithosphere that forms the moving plates.

questions.stem: Which comparison of the mechanisms that drive plate movement is correct?
options: Mantle convection is primary; slab pull is strongest; ridge push is secondary.
Slab pull is primary; ridge push is strongest; mantle convection is secondary.
Ridge push is primary; mantle convection is strongest; slab pull is secondary.
Mantle convection, slab pull and ridge push are equally important.
questions.explanation: Mantle convection is the primary driver, while the sinking of a dense oceanic slab provides the strongest force. Ridge push has a smaller contribution.

questions.stem: Which observation provides the most direct evidence of seafloor spreading, supporting the movement of oceanic plates?
options: A central rift at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where new oceanic crust forms.
An ocean trench beside an oceanic plate that is subducting.
A volcanic island arc where two oceanic plates converge.
Fold mountains formed where two continental plates collide.
questions.explanation: The central rift and formation of new oceanic crust at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge show that plates are moving apart. Trenches, island arcs and fold mountains instead indicate convergent boundaries.

questions.stem: A transform plate boundary is shown where two plates slide horizontally past one another. Which statement best describes this boundary?
options: Plates collide, destroying crust and producing volcanoes and trenches
Plates separate, creating new crust and forming mid-ocean ridges
Crust is neither created nor destroyed; shallow, frequent earthquakes occur without volcanoes
Plates slide past, creating new crust at a mid-ocean ridge with common volcanoes
questions.explanation: C is correct because transform boundaries are conservative: plates slide past laterally, so no crust is created or destroyed, and earthquakes are shallow and frequent without volcanoes. Option A describes a convergent boundary.

questions.stem: At a convergent (destructive) plate boundary, two plates move towards one another. Which combination of features is most likely to develop?
options: Volcanoes, trenches and earthquakes
Mid-ocean ridges, new crust and undersea volcanoes
Fault lines, shallow frequent earthquakes and no volcanoes
Separation of plates, crust creation and divergent ridges
questions.explanation: A is correct because convergent boundaries involve collision, commonly producing volcanoes, trenches and earthquakes. Option B describes a divergent (constructive) boundary, where plates move apart and new crust forms.

questions.stem: A crustal block moves downward relative to an adjacent block along a fracture. Which force and fault type best explain this movement?
options: A Compressional force; reverse fault
B Tensional force; normal fault
C Shearing force; transform fault
D Compressional force; transform fault
questions.explanation: Tensional pulling stretches and thins rocks, producing normal faulting, in which one block drops. Compressional force causes reverse faulting, where one block is pushed up.

questions.stem: Compressional force acts on layered rocks, which bend rather than break. Which sequence correctly shows the conversion of force into a geological process and landform?
options: A Force builds up → rock cannot bend → rock breaks → fault line forms
B Compressional force → folding → anticline or syncline → fold mountains
C Tensional force → normal faulting → one block drops → rift valley forms
D Shearing force → transform faulting → blocks slide past → fault line forms
questions.explanation: Compressional force squeezes rock layers, causing them to bend into anticlines or synclines and eventually form fold mountains. Option A describes faulting, which occurs when rock cannot bend and therefore breaks.

questions.stem: Figure 1 shows a cross-section of rock layers bent into an arch curving upward. Which option correctly identifies the fold and the force responsible?
options: Syncline; compressional force
Anticline; compressional force
Monocline; tensional force
Anticline; tensional force
questions.explanation: An upward arch is an anticline, formed when compressional forces squeeze and bend rock layers. Option A is incorrect because a syncline dips downward, while C and D incorrectly associate the fold with tensional force or a single bend.

questions.stem: Which option correctly distinguishes the effects of tensional and compressional forces on rock?
options: Tensional forces break and displace rock, while compressional forces squeeze, bend and wrinkle rock layers.
Tensional forces squeeze, bend and wrinkle rock layers, while compressional forces break and displace rock.
Both types of force primarily bend rock layers without breaking or displacing them.
Tensional forces build new rock layers, while compressional forces remove them through erosion.
questions.explanation: Tensional forces cause rock to break and displace, whereas compressional forces squeeze rock layers, making them bend and wrinkle. Option B reverses these effects, while C and D incorrectly describe processes that do not distinguish the two forces.

questions.stem: Figure 1 shows folded rock layers in cross-section. The layers in the middle curve upwards, while those on either side dip away from the centre. Which fold is at the centre?
options: Anticline
Syncline
Fault line
Rift valley
questions.explanation: An anticline is an upward fold of rock layers. A syncline bends downwards, so it does not describe the central upward arch.

questions.stem: The Indo-Australian Plate collides with the Eurasian Plate. Why do fold mountains such as the Himalayas form rather than a deep-ocean trench?
options: Both plates are continental and similar in density, so neither subducts; compression folds and uplifts sedimentary layers.
The Indo-Australian Plate is denser and subducts beneath Eurasia, producing a deep-ocean trench.
The plates slide horizontally past each other, and shearing produces a transform fault line.
The plates move apart, and the crust stretches to form a rift valley.
questions.explanation: The Himalayas formed through continental-continental collision, where compression folded and uplifted the sedimentary layers because neither plate subducted. Subduction at an oceanic-continental boundary would instead tend to form a trench and volcanoes.

questions.stem: Which fault type and rock movement result from shearing forces?
options: Normal fault: tension pulls the crust apart and the central block sinks.
Reverse fault: compression pushes one block upward relative to the other.
Strike-slip fault: blocks slide horizontally past each other.
Transform fault: blocks move vertically as the central block sinks.
questions.explanation: Shearing causes rocks to grind horizontally, producing strike-slip or transform faults, such as the San Andreas Fault. Normal faulting is associated with tension, while reverse faulting is associated with compression, so A and B do not describe shearing.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly explains the formation of a rift valley in continental crust?
options: Tension pulls the crust apart; normal faults form, and the central block sinks as a graben between uplifted horsts.
Compression shortens the crust; reverse faults form, and the central block rises as a horst between down-dropped grabens.
Tension pulls the crust apart; transform faults form, and adjacent blocks slide horizontally past each other.
Shearing grinds the crust horizontally; normal faults form, and the central block sinks between uplifted horsts.
questions.explanation: Tension stretches and fractures continental crust, producing parallel normal faults and a down-dropped central graben, creating a rift valley such as the East African Rift Valley. B wrongly associates tension with compression, while C and D confuse shearing with the tensional process.

questions.stem: A volcanic eruption occurs along a long crack in the Earth's crust. Which combination best describes this eruption?
options: A vent eruption producing usually explosive activity
A fissure eruption through a single central opening
A fissure eruption producing fluid basaltic lava
A vent eruption forming mainly from ejected volcanic ash
questions.explanation: A fissure eruption occurs along linear cracks and generally produces fluid basaltic lava through effusive activity. Option A is incorrect because a single central opening and frequent explosivity are characteristic of a vent eruption.

questions.stem: The Hawaiian Islands formed above a stationary mantle plume as the Pacific Plate moved northwest. Which statement correctly describes the island chain?
options: The youngest island is in the northwest and the oldest is over the hot spot
All the islands formed simultaneously when the Pacific Plate passed over the hot spot
The islands are the oldest in the northwest and the youngest in the southeast
The hot spot moved northwest together with the Pacific Plate
questions.explanation: As the Pacific Plate moves northwest over a stationary hot spot, new volcanoes form above the plume while older volcanoes move away and become extinct. Thus, the Emperor Seamounts in the northwest are older, while the Big Island over the hot spot is youngest.

questions.stem: An oceanic plate moves towards a continental plate. Which sequence correctly describes the subduction process and the landforms produced?
options: Subduction, magma generation, volcanoes, an ocean trench and fold mountains
Subduction, magma generation, a volcanic island arc and fold mountains
The continental plate subducts, forming volcanoes but no ocean trench
Both plates collide without subduction, forming only fold mountains
questions.explanation: The denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate, forming an ocean trench, while rising magma produces volcanoes and compresses and uplifts the continental crust into fold mountains. Without subduction, as at a continental–continental boundary, volcanoes and an ocean trench would not form.

questions.stem: Two oceanic plates move towards each other at a convergent boundary. The older, denser plate subducts beneath the younger plate. Which landform is most likely to form?
options: A volcanic island arc arranged parallel to the trench
A continental fold mountain range formed by crustal compression
A volcanic mountain range rising on a continental plate
A deep V-shaped ocean trench without volcanic islands
questions.explanation: At an oceanic–oceanic convergent boundary, subduction generates magma that rises to form an arc-shaped chain of volcanic islands. A fold mountain range without subduction is characteristic of continental–continental collision, not oceanic–oceanic collision.

questions.stem: At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, which sequence best explains how new oceanic crust is formed?
options: Plates move apart → decompression melting → magma upwells → new oceanic crust forms
Plates move together → magma rises → new oceanic crust forms at the ridge crest
Plates move apart → oceanic crust subducts → magma forms new crust
Plates remain stationary → tension creates a gap → new oceanic crust forms
questions.explanation: At a divergent boundary, plates move apart and decompression melting produces magma, which rises and forms new oceanic crust at the ridge crest. Option B is incorrect because plates move towards each other at convergent boundaries, causing subduction.

questions.stem: How does tensional force produce a rift valley in continental crust?
options: Normal faulting lowers a central block, forming a graben between uplifted horsts
Normal faulting raises a central block, forming a horst between lowered blocks
Compression folds the central block upwards, with magma rising along the faults
A hotspot lifts the crust, creating a central ridge bounded by fault scarps
questions.explanation: Tension pulls the crust apart, causing parallel normal faults and the sinking of the central block, or graben, to form a rift valley. Option B is incorrect because the central block is downdropped, while the flanking horsts are uplifted.

questions.stem: At a conservative (transform) plate boundary, which sequence best explains why earthquakes are frequent?
options: Plates slide past each other; friction locks them, stress builds, and sudden release causes an earthquake.
Plates move apart; magma rises, and its movement causes earthquakes.
Plates collide; one subducts, and the subducting plate causes earthquakes.
Plates slide smoothly past each other without friction or sudden movement.
questions.explanation: Friction locks transform plates, allowing stress to accumulate before it is suddenly released as an earthquake. B is wrong because plates at a transform boundary slide past rather than move apart.

questions.stem: Why are volcanoes generally absent at conservative (transform) plate boundaries?
options: No magma is generated because there is neither subduction nor decompression melting.
The plates move apart, causing magma to form by decompression melting.
Friction between the plates heats the crust until magma forms.
One plate subducts beneath the other, generating magma below the fault.
questions.explanation: Transform boundaries involve horizontal sliding, with no subduction or plate separation, so magma is not generated and volcanoes are absent. B is wrong because transform plates slide past rather than move apart.

questions.stem: The Hawaiian Islands form a volcanic chain as the Pacific Plate moves over a stationary mantle plume. Which statement correctly describes the chain’s age progression?
options: The oldest islands are in the northwest, while the Big Island is youngest and lies over the hot spot.
The oldest islands are in the southeast, while the Big Island is youngest and lies over the hot spot.
The oldest and youngest islands are both located directly over the hot spot.
The Big Island is oldest, while islands in the northwest are the youngest.
questions.explanation: As the Pacific Plate moves northwest over the stationary hot spot, newly formed volcanoes are carried away and become extinct. Therefore, islands become progressively older towards the northwest; option B wrongly reverses this age progression.
questions.subtopic_title: Intraplate volcanism: hot spots and mantle plumes

questions.stem: The Hawaiian Islands form far from any plate boundary. Which process best explains the origin of the islands and the continued creation of the volcanic chain?
options: A mantle plume rises, forming volcanoes as the Pacific Plate moves northwest over the stationary hot spot.
Oceanic crust subducts beneath continental crust, causing melting and forming a volcanic island arc.
Seafloor spreading at a divergent boundary creates oceanic crust and a chain of volcanic islands.
Repeated fissure eruptions along one long crack in oceanic crust produce the Hawaiian volcanic chain.
questions.explanation: The Hawaiian chain is an example of intraplate volcanism: a mantle plume supplies magma while the Pacific Plate moves over the stationary hot spot. Option C is incorrect because the Hawaiian Islands are not formed at a divergent plate boundary.
questions.subtopic_title: Intraplate volcanism: hot spots and mantle plumes

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the movement of the Nazca Plate?
options: Eastward away from the East Pacific Rise
Westward towards the Pacific Plate
Northwestward beneath the South American Plate
Southwestward towards the Antarctic Plate
questions.explanation: The Nazca Plate moves northwestwards and is subducted beneath the South American Plate at a destructive (convergent) boundary, producing the Andes.

questions.stem: A volcano has steep sides of about 30° and alternating layers of lava and ash. Which type is it?
options: Shield volcano
Composite volcano
Cinder cone
Fissure eruption
questions.explanation: Composite volcanoes have steep sides and alternating lava and ash layers, and their viscous magma traps gas, producing highly explosive eruptions. A shield volcano is incorrect because it has gentle slopes and fluid basaltic lava.

questions.stem: Before the 1991 eruption of Pinatubo in the Philippines, warnings were issued. Which action most directly saved lives?
options: Constructing lava barriers around the volcano
Diverting lava away from settlements
Evacuating more than 60,000 people
Restricting tourist access to the crater
questions.explanation: Early warnings enabled the evacuation of more than 60,000 people, helping to save thousands of lives. Lava barriers were used in Iceland, while lava diversion was used at Kīlauea in Hawaii.

questions.stem: At a transform plate boundary, why are earthquakes generally strong and frequent?
options: Plates move apart slowly, so there is little stress accumulation and only small earthquakes.
Plates collide or subduct, causing massive strain to accumulate before a very powerful release.
Plates slide horizontally past each other; friction locks them, builds stress, and sudden releases produce frequent earthquakes.
Plates move apart rapidly, causing shallow earthquakes of moderate intensity but little stress accumulation.
questions.explanation: At transform boundaries, constantly grinding plates become locked by friction, so stress builds and is released suddenly, causing strong and frequent earthquakes. Option B describes convergent boundaries, where collision or subduction accumulates strain.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between an earthquake's focus, epicentre and seismic waves?
options: The focus is on the surface directly above the epicentre, and seismic waves originate there.
The focus is underground, the epicentre is directly above it, and seismic waves travel outward from the focus.
The focus and epicentre are the same underground point, and seismic waves form only along the fault line.
The focus is the crack where movement occurs, while the epicentre is where strain begins.
questions.explanation: The focus is the underground point where the earthquake starts, while the epicentre is the surface point directly above it. Seismic waves travel outward from the focus; option D wrongly confuses the focus with the fault line and strain.

questions.stem: After a submarine earthquake, which sequence best describes how a tsunami warning is communicated to the public?
options: Buoys → TV, radio and phones → seafloor sensors → warning centres
Seafloor sensors → coastal landslide → warning centres → TV, radio and phones
Seafloor sensors → DART buoys → warning centres → TV, radio and phones
Volcanic eruption → DART buoys → coastal cliff → seafloor sensors
questions.explanation: Seafloor sensors detect earthquakes, DART buoys support tsunami detection, and warning centres such as PTWC issue warnings communicated through television, radio and phones. The other sequences include processes or components that do not form the warning chain.

questions.stem: Which observation most strongly indicates that a submarine earthquake has generated a tsunami?
options: The seabed moves horizontally along a fault.
The seabed moves vertically, pushing the water above it upwards or downwards.
Magma erupts through a single opening on the seafloor.
Rock debris falls from a coastal cliff into the ocean.
questions.explanation: A tsunami-generating earthquake requires vertical seabed movement, which pushes the overlying water and generates waves. Horizontal movement does not cause a tsunami, while the other processes describe volcanic eruptions and landslides.

questions.stem: Which combination represents the widest effective approach to reducing tsunami losses through land-use planning, preparedness and building measures?
options: Install buoys and warning centres, but do not prepare evacuation routes or regulate coastal construction
Mark evacuation routes and shelters only, without using hazard maps or flood-resistant building codes
Use hazard maps for land-use zoning, provide clear routes to high ground, and require flood-resistant coastal building codes
Construct sea walls and breakwaters only, without public education, evacuation planning or building controls
questions.explanation: This combination reduces exposure through land-use zoning, enables rapid evacuation, and limits damage to buildings designed for flooding. Option A is the main distractor because detection and warning alone cannot protect people who lack evacuation routes or safe buildings.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly explains how an earthquake early warning system provides advance notice of damaging shaking?
options: Detect P-waves → calculate the earthquake's location and magnitude → issue an alert before S-waves arrive
Detect S-waves → calculate the earthquake's location and magnitude → issue an alert after surface shaking begins
Measure gas emissions → detect ground deformation → issue an alert before volcanic tremors occur
Observe a tsunami at sea → issue an alert → evacuate people to coastal shelters
questions.explanation: P-waves travel faster and are less damaging than S-waves, so detecting them allows warnings seconds before the damaging S-waves arrive. Option B is wrong because it reverses the sequence: warning after S-waves arrive would provide no useful advance notice.

questions.stem: Figure 1 shows two adjacent drainage basins separated by a line. Rainwater collects within each basin, tributaries join the main river, and the river eventually enters the sea. What is the separating line?
options: The catchment area
The confluence
The mouth
The watershed
questions.explanation: The watershed is the boundary between drainage basins. The catchment area is where precipitation collects, while the confluence and mouth are locations where rivers meet and enter the sea respectively.

questions.stem: Figure 2 describes the Shing Mun River from its upper catchment to its lower reaches. Which sequence best matches its long-profile features?
options: Upper: gentle gradient and deposition; lower: steep gradient and vertical erosion
Upper: steep gradient and vertical erosion; lower: gentle gradient and deposition, with fast flow in a concrete channel
Upper: steep gradient and vertical erosion; lower: gentle gradient and deposition, with slow flow in a concrete channel
Upper: steep gradient and deposition; lower: gentle gradient and vertical erosion
questions.explanation: The upper course has a steep gradient and strong vertical erosion, while deposition dominates in the gentle lower course. Unlike option C, the Shing Mun River’s concrete lower channel maintains fast flow rather than slow flow.

questions.stem: The Shing Mun River has a steep upper catchment with many boulders, while its lower reaches have a smoother concrete channel and a larger cross-sectional area. Which factors best explain the faster flow in the lower reaches?
options: Lower roughness reduces friction, while a higher hydraulic radius makes the flow more efficient.
Higher discharge and a larger cross-sectional area directly cause the water to flow faster.
A steeper gradient and lower roughness both increase velocity in the lower reaches.
Greater depth and higher roughness increase the lower channel’s velocity.
questions.explanation: The smoother concrete channel has lower roughness, while its larger cross-section gives a higher hydraulic radius, allowing more efficient and faster flow. B confuses discharge, the volume of water passing a point, with velocity.

questions.stem: Within a meandering river channel, where is erosion most likely to occur, and what is the main reason?
options: At the outside bend, where energy is concentrated.
At the inside bend, where energy is concentrated.
At the inside bend, where low energy causes deposition.
At the outside bend, where low energy causes deposition.
questions.explanation: Energy is higher at the outside bend, making this the most likely location of erosion and river-cliff formation. C describes the low-energy inside bend, where deposition forms a point bar instead.

questions.stem: At a coastal cave, wave pressure repeatedly compresses air in cracks, gradually widening them. Which erosion process and landform are correctly paired?
options: A Hydraulic action; cave
B Abrasion; cliff
C Attrition; cave
D Solution; cliff
questions.explanation: Hydraulic action involves compressed air in cracks, helping to widen them and form a cave. Abrasion (B) instead occurs when sand and pebbles wear against rock like sandpaper.

questions.stem: During a flood, sand grains bounce along the river bed in a series of short jumps before settling on a point bar. Which transportation process and depositional landform are correctly paired?
options: A Traction; point bar
B Saltation; point bar
C Saltation; levee
D Suspension; point bar
questions.explanation: Saltation is the bouncing movement of sediment grains along a river bed, while a point bar forms where sediment is deposited. Traction (A) involves larger particles rolling or sliding along the bed.

questions.stem: Figure 1 shows a former river meander cut off from the main channel. A lake occupies the abandoned meander on a flat floodplain, where deposition has occurred. Which landform is shown?
options: Oxbow lake
Active meander
V-shaped valley
Waterfall
questions.explanation: An oxbow lake forms when the meander neck is cut off, leaving a lake in the former channel on the floodplain. An active meander remains connected to the river and is not an abandoned, sediment-filled section.

questions.stem: Figure 1 shows a river channel bordered by raised, sediment-built embankments. The embankments stand above the flat land on both sides of the river. Which landform is shown?
options: Levee
Floodplain
Delta
Oxbow lake
questions.explanation: A levee is a natural embankment formed by sediment buildup along the river bank, standing above the floodplain. A floodplain is the flat land beside the channel rather than the raised embankment itself.

questions.stem: A community seeks a relatively lower-cost strategy that works with natural river processes and accepts regular maintenance. Which combination is most suitable?
options: A Dams, levees and channelisation
B Reservoirs, dams and flood walls
C Wetland restoration, afforestation and floodplain management
D Channelisation, reservoir construction and flood walls
questions.explanation: Wetland restoration, afforestation and floodplain management are soft-engineering measures that are environmentally friendly and work with natural processes. Although hard engineering such as channelisation acts immediately and lasts longer, it has high costs and can be environmentally harmful.

questions.stem: A flood-prone urban river urgently needs measures that take effect immediately and provide long-lasting protection. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: A Raise levees and construct flood walls
B Restore wetlands and floodplain management
C Afforest catchments to slow surface runoff
D Install forecasting, public alerts and evacuation plans
questions.explanation: Levees and flood walls are hard-engineering measures, which take effect immediately and are generally long-lasting. The other options are softer approaches: restoration and afforestation act gradually, while early warning helps people respond but does not directly reduce flooding.

questions.stem: Which pair of conditions and beach outcome correctly describes constructive waves?
options: Low, gentle waves; sediment is deposited and the beach is built.
High, powerful waves; sediment is deposited and the beach is built.
Low, gentle waves; sand is removed from the beach.
High, powerful waves; waves break more gently and build the beach.
questions.explanation: Constructive waves are low and gentle, so they deposit sediment and build beaches. Option B describes destructive waves, which are high and powerful and erode beaches.

questions.stem: Winds blow steadily across a long fetch before reaching a coastal area. What is the likely effect on wave energy?
options: Wave energy is low because energy is lost over a long fetch.
Wave energy is high because both fetch and wind speed increase wave energy.
Wave energy is unchanged because only wind speed affects wave energy.
Wave energy is high because a shorter fetch and stronger winds transfer more energy.
questions.explanation: Wave energy increases with both fetch and wind speed, so strong winds travelling over a long stretch of water produce energetic waves. Option C is incorrect because fetch also affects wave energy.

questions.stem: A narrow ridge of deposited sediment connects the mainland to an offshore island. Name this landform and the process responsible for forming it.
options: Tombolo; deposition by longshore drift
Spit; deposition by longshore drift
Tombolo; removal by longshore drift
Bar; deposition by longshore drift
questions.explanation: A tombolo is a deposited sediment ridge linking the mainland to an offshore island, and longshore drift can supply the sediment. A spit extends from the coast without joining an island, while a bar develops roughly parallel to the shoreline.

questions.stem: A rocky coast now contains a sea cliff, wave-cut platform, cave, arch, isolated sea stack and stump. Which sequence best shows the usual development of these coastal erosional landforms?
options: Sea cliff → wave-cut platform → cave → arch → stack → stump
Sea cliff → cave → wave-cut platform → arch → stack → stump
Wave-cut platform → sea cliff → cave → arch → stack → stump
Sea cliff → wave-cut platform → arch → cave → stack → stump
questions.explanation: Continued wave erosion retreats the sea cliff and leaves a wave-cut platform; caves then enlarge into arches, stacks and finally stumps. Option B is incorrect because the wave-cut platform forms as the cliff retreats, before the cave develops into an arch.

questions.stem: Figure 1 shows a beach where waves approach obliquely. The swash carries sand up the beach at an angle, while the backwash moves down the beach under gravity. Which movement best describes the resulting sediment transport?
options: Sand travels in a straight line parallel to the shoreline.
Sand moves up and down in a zigzag, with net movement along the shoreline.
Sand moves directly offshore and is never deposited on the beach.
Sand moves in a complete circle without any net coastal transport.
questions.explanation: The oblique swash and the steeper, shore-perpendicular backwash create a zigzag movement that produces net transport along the coast. Option A is wrong because individual movements are not simply parallel to the shoreline.

questions.stem: Figure 2 shows a straight beach where waves approach obliquely from the west and abundant sediment is available. In which general direction should net longshore drift occur, and which factor mainly controls it?
options: Eastward; the direction from which the waves approach.
Westward; the amount of sediment available.
Eastward; the amount of sediment available only.
Westward; the beach orientation alone.
questions.explanation: The direction of approaching waves determines the direction of longshore drift, so waves from the west produce net movement eastward. The amount of sediment affects how much material is transported, not the main direction of drift.

questions.stem: A Hong Kong coast faces erosion, storm-surge flooding and sea-level rise. Which statement best evaluates using sea walls together with beach nourishment?
options: Sea walls provide immediate protection, while beach nourishment is environmentally friendly but needs regular maintenance; both may involve high costs.
Sea walls are environmentally friendly and work with natural processes, while beach nourishment provides durable, maintenance-free protection.
Beach nourishment is the only suitable measure because sea walls cannot protect against wave attack or flooding.
Sea walls are the only suitable measure because they are cheap, visually attractive and cannot increase erosion elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Sea walls are effective in the short term and provide immediate protection, but they are expensive and may increase erosion elsewhere. Beach nourishment works with natural processes and has a natural appearance, but it requires regular maintenance and may be costly over time.

questions.stem: A Hong Kong coastal community wants to reduce wave attack and interrupt sediment moving along the shore. Which measures perform these functions?
options: Sea wall and groyne
Breakwater and revetment
Groyne and breakwater
Revetment and sea wall
questions.explanation: A sea wall prevents wave attack, while a groyne interrupts longshore drift. Breakwaters absorb wave energy, whereas revetments are sloped stone or concrete defences, so options B and D do not match the stated functions.

questions.stem: A Hong Kong coastal area is vulnerable to flooding. Which option correctly applies the three-pronged approach and classifies coastal engineering measures?
options: Avoid new development; reduce vulnerability through management; protect with a seawall. Seawall is hard; beach nourishment is soft and requires replenishment.
Avoid vulnerable areas by building coastal defences; reduce vulnerability by prohibiting development; protect the coast through beach nourishment.
Avoid erosion by replenishing beach sand; reduce flooding risk by constructing a seawall; protect vulnerable areas by restricting development.
Avoid flooding by reducing vulnerability through management; reduce erosion by building coastal defences; protect vulnerable areas by prohibiting development.
questions.explanation: The three-pronged approach is to avoid development in vulnerable areas, reduce vulnerability through management and protect the coast with defences such as seawalls. Seawalls are hard engineering measures, whereas beach nourishment is a soft measure that must be replenished; option B wrongly assigns these actions.

questions.stem: Under the progressive principle, a coastal facility can be improved in stages as conditions change. Which design response best reflects this approach while accounting for climate change?
options: Include projected sea-level rise in the design now, allowing greater resilience and future upgrades.
Use present-day sea level only, because progressive improvement can address later sea-level rise.
Delay all protective works until sea level has risen by about 1.2 metres.
Adopt a fixed facility height based on current conditions, with no provision for later changes.
questions.explanation: The progressive principle accommodates changing conditions, while Hong Kong’s design requirements include projected sea-level rise of about 1.2 metres by 2100 under a high-emission scenario. Option B is incorrect because ignoring this rise in the initial design would weaken the facility’s future resilience.

questions.stem: A Hong Kong coastal area uses seawalls and beach nourishment to reduce erosion and flooding risk. Which evaluation best reflects the effectiveness of these measures?
options: A Seawalls protect land directly, while nourishment restores sediment; both should be assessed by cost, environmental impact and sustainability.
B Both schemes are fully sustainable because they permanently stop all wave energy and sediment movement along the coast.
C Beach nourishment is always preferable because it has no maintenance cost and does not alter the natural coastal system.
D Seawalls are ineffective because they enhance deposition, while beach nourishment can only widen a beach temporarily.
questions.explanation: Hard management such as seawalls directly protects the coast, while soft management such as beach nourishment replenishes sediment. Their effectiveness should be evaluated against cost, environmental impact and sustainability, rather than claiming that they completely halt coastal processes.

questions.stem: Which option correctly matches a notable Hong Kong coastal landform with its location?
options: A High Island — hexagonal rock columns
B Ninepin Group — hexagonal rock columns
C Sai Kung Peninsula — largest island in Hong Kong
D Lantau — volcanic island group
questions.explanation: High Island is renowned for its hexagonal rock columns. The main distractor is incorrect because the Ninepin Group is a group of volcanic islands, while Lantau is Hong Kong's largest island.

questions.stem: After China’s Reform and Opening, why did export-oriented manufacturing concentrate in Special Economic Zones such as Shenzhen?
options: Policy incentives attracted foreign investment, while coastal port access lowered the cost of exporting products.
Nearby iron ore and coal reduced transport costs because these raw materials are bulky and lose weight.
Low wages were the only major advantage, and Special Economic Zone status was unrelated to industrial location.
Military contracts during the Cold War guaranteed factories in these zones a continuing supply of government orders.
questions.explanation: Special Economic Zones combined policy incentives with access to export ports, helping attract foreign investment and reduce export transport costs. Option C overstates the role of cheap labour because capital and labour are footloose, while policy and market access determine the created advantage.

questions.stem: Which explanation best shows how a historical factor can keep an established defence industry in a particular location?
options: The firm won military contracts during the Cold War, and continued government orders support remaining at its established base.
The firm is close to iron ore and coal because these bulky materials lose weight during transport, reducing production costs.
The industry is footloose, so the firm can relocate easily whenever another location offers lower wages.
The firm stays in an industrial park because government subsidies reduce the cost of its land and facilities.
questions.explanation: Military contracts secured during the Cold War are a historical location factor that can create industrial inertia, explaining why the industry remains at an established base. Government subsidies in option D may also influence location, but they do not explain the specific historical factor described.

questions.stem: A new electric arc furnace steelworks opens in coastal China, while some inland mills decline. Which explanation best matches the technology-driven shift of the 2020s?
options: Coastal EAFs benefit from energy prices, environmental compliance and port access; hydrogen DRI can instead favour renewable-rich inland regions
Coastal EAFs rely mainly on cheap labour, while industrial inertia ensures that declining inland mills will never close
Inland EAFs dominate because ore is always cheaper to transport than finished steel, and labour costs remain decisive
All new steel capacity remains inland to exploit local coal, since coastal plants cannot meet environmental standards
questions.explanation: A is correct because new coastal EAF capacity is influenced by energy price, environmental compliance and port access, while renewable-powered hydrogen DRI may favour inland regions. B is wrong because automation reduces the importance of cheap labour, and inertia delays rather than prevents inland closures.

questions.stem: Which option correctly states the dominant location factors shaping China's iron and steel industry from pre-1949 to the 2020s?
options: Pre-1949: materials/ports; 1949–78: materials and planning, with defence setting the inland bias; post-1978: export markets and incentives; WDS: policy/infrastructure; 2020s: energy, compliance and ports
Pre-1949: defence; 1949–78: defence at each site; post-1978: cheap labour; WDS: export markets; 2020s: raw materials alone
Pre-1949: cheap labour; 1949–78: coastal ports; post-1978: defence; WDS: foreign capital; 2020s: cheap labour
Pre-1949: automation; 1949–78: export markets; post-1978: defence; WDS: raw materials only; 2020s: coastal location and compliance
questions.explanation: A correctly distinguishes each period: defence explains the inland direction after 1949, not the choice of individual steel centres. B is wrong because raw materials and state planning determined those sites, while cheap labour did not dominate post-1978 or 2020s location.

questions.stem: Which combination best explains why headquarters and research and development activities remain concentrated in Silicon Valley rather than moving to lower-wage locations?
options: Pleasant climate and local silicon resources
Low wages and abundant industrial land
Cold War defence contracts and reverse brain drain
Stanford research, venture capital, skilled labour and firm agglomeration
questions.explanation: Stanford University provides research and a talent pipeline, while venture capital, skilled labour and entrepreneurial culture sustain innovation. Agglomeration links firms, suppliers and services, reinforcing concentration. Historical defence contracts and reverse brain drain helped establish the industry, but local silicon is no longer used and climate is not the main factor.
questions.subtopic_title: Silicon Valley as a global IT centre

questions.stem: Why does a transnational IT company commonly adopt multi-point production, locating design, chip fabrication and assembly in different countries?
options: Locate every stage in the United States to minimise transport costs
Locate every stage in one Asian country to maximise agglomeration economies
Locate design in low-wage countries and fabrication in the headquarters country
Locate each stage where its required skills, capital, infrastructure and labour costs are most favourable
questions.explanation: Multi-point production assigns each stage to its most favourable location: design in the US benefits from skilled labour and intellectual property protection, while fabrication and assembly use Asian capital infrastructure and relatively low-cost labour. Keeping every stage in one country, as suggested by A and B, ignores these stage-specific advantages.
questions.subtopic_title: Silicon Valley as a global IT centre

questions.stem: Which sequence best demonstrates cumulative causation in an industrial cluster?
options: A port attracts firms; this creates a skilled labour pool, knowledge spillovers and shared infrastructure, whose lower costs attract still more firms.
A port attracts firms, but further growth depends entirely on a new government policy because agglomeration economies are exhausted.
Firms first develop shared infrastructure and a skilled labour pool, and only then does an initial advantage draw related industries into the area.
Firms cluster mainly to avoid congestion, rising rents and competition for staff, so clustering strengthens itself without reducing costs.
questions.explanation: Cumulative causation is a self-reinforcing process in which an initial advantage creates growth, and each round of growth makes the next round more likely. Option B wrongly makes a new external cause necessary, while C reverses the causal sequence.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly explains agglomeration economies and a limit of industrial clustering?
options: Internal economies save individual firms costs through local linkages; external economies come from shared facilities and labour; rising rents and congestion may eventually outweigh these benefits.
Internal economies are benefits for the wider region, while external economies are cost savings enjoyed only by individual firms within the cluster.
Shared roads, power and utilities are internal economies, whereas skilled workers moving between firms are external economies; congestion has no effect on clustering.
Industrial clustering always lowers firms’ costs because rising land prices and competition for staff are outweighed by unlimited agglomeration economies.
questions.explanation: Internal economies provide cost savings for individual clustered firms, whereas external economies benefit firms through shared infrastructure and a pooled labour market. Clustering can eventually create diseconomies such as high rents and congestion, so its benefits are not unlimited.

questions.stem: A transnational corporation (TNC) is headquartered in one country but produces goods or services in another. Which option correctly explains why a TNC may set up production in a less developed country (LDC)?
options: Lower labour costs can reduce the wage share of unit costs, lowering unit costs and improving price competitiveness.
The TNC sets up in an LDC mainly because its stronger infrastructure lowers transport costs.
The TNC sets up in an LDC because local consumers create less demand, reducing the need for production.
The TNC sets up in an LDC because stricter local labour and environmental rules reduce its costs.
questions.explanation: A is correct because a lower wage share of unit costs can reduce unit costs and make the TNC's products more price-competitive. B confuses an impact of TNC investment with a location reason, while C and D reverse the effects of growing markets and looser regulations.

questions.stem: An LDC hosts a TNC that creates jobs, transfers skills and technology, and builds infrastructure. However, many inputs are imported and profits are repatriated. Which evaluation is best supported?
options: Short-run benefits are significant, but long-run dependency may increase if local skills and suppliers do not develop.
The TNC's presence automatically creates strong local linkages, making dependence on foreign capital unlikely.
Technology transfer means profits must eventually remain in the host country.
Increases in export earnings and employment mean the host country cannot become dependent on foreign capital.
questions.explanation: A correctly weighs jobs, technology and infrastructure against dependency and profits leaving the host country. D is wrong because employment and export earnings can coexist with dependency when imported inputs and repatriated profits limit local economic linkages.

questions.stem: Hong Kong’s factories have closed and employment has shifted towards services. Which statement correctly distinguishes the short-run consequences from the long-run consequences of deindustrialization?
options: Short run: factory closures immediately create a mature service economy. Long run: displaced workers face no adjustment.
Short run: factory closures cause some job losses. Long run: services expand, while retraining and new industry absorb part of the workforce.
Short run: all displaced workers immediately transfer into finance and tourism. Long run: government intervention becomes unnecessary.
Short run: Hong Kong’s manufacturing base remains unchanged. Long run: services gradually replace manufacturing without any disruption.
questions.explanation: Factory closures can initially cause unemployment and retraining needs, while the longer-term response is a shift towards higher-value services, with retraining and new industry absorbing some workers. Displaced workers cannot all move immediately into services because their existing skills may not match service-sector jobs.

questions.stem: Hong Kong’s manufacturing wage advantage disappeared after industrial wages rose. Which causal chain best explains why factories subsequently relocated to the Pearl River Delta?
options: Automation made it impossible for Hong Kong factories to remain internationally competitive.
Rising wages removed Hong Kong’s cheap-labour advantage, so firms relocated factories to lower-wage locations in the PRD.
Globalisation increased transport and communication costs, making export-oriented manufacturing unviable in Hong Kong.
Competition from less developed countries raised demand for Hong Kong products, encouraging factories to expand.
questions.explanation: Rising labour costs reversed the location factor that originally attracted manufacturing to Hong Kong: firms followed cheaper labour to the PRD. Automation may reduce labour needs and encourage plant consolidation, but it does not make Hong Kong manufacturing inherently uncompetitive.

questions.stem: Hong Kong proposes installing solar panels on public-housing roofs. Which evaluation best uses the three pillars to judge whether the measure is genuinely sustainable?
options: It weighs installation and maintenance costs, emission cuts, resident savings and equitable access, while noting trade-offs.
It reduces carbon emissions, so the measure is sustainable because its environmental benefits outweigh every economic and social cost.
It creates local jobs and lowers electricity bills, so the measure is sustainable because its economic benefits are greatest.
It improves housing quality, so the measure is sustainable because social gains justify any pressure on resources or public funds.
questions.explanation: Option A checks economic affordability and maintenance, environmental benefits, and social access and participation, while recognising trade-offs. Option B wrongly equates sustainability with environmental improvement and ignores the other pillars.

questions.stem: Which statement gives the Brundtland definition of sustainable development verbatim?
options: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Development that meets the needs of the present while conserving natural resources for future generations.
Development that balances economic growth, environmental protection and social equity in the present.
Development that enables future generations to meet their needs without reducing current living standards.
questions.explanation: This is the Brundtland definition, linking present needs with the capacity of future generations to meet their own needs. Option C describes the three-pillar idea but is not the definition verbatim.

questions.stem: In a Hong Kong urban area, congestion causes air pollution. Which causal chain best explains how this pollution creates a social cost?
options: Slow-moving vehicles emit more pollutants, worsening air quality and increasing pressure on healthcare services.
Air pollution reduces the number of vehicles, easing congestion and improving workers’ health.
Higher property prices force more people to drive, directly increasing air pollution and hospital admissions.
Waste collection vehicles become less efficient during congestion, causing more industrial emissions.
questions.explanation: Congestion lengthens journeys and increases idling, allowing more vehicle emissions to accumulate. The resulting poorer air quality creates social costs through health problems and greater demand for healthcare; option B reverses the causal relationship.

questions.stem: Why are a housing shortage and high property prices essentially the same urban problem in a land-scarce city?
options: When housing demand exceeds the limited housing supply, fewer homes are available and prices rise.
High property prices always create additional homes, so shortages and high prices cannot occur together.
Housing shortages cause property prices to fall because potential buyers can afford more homes.
A housing shortage is an environmental problem, while high property prices are only an economic issue.
questions.explanation: In a land-scarce city, limited land constrains housing supply while demand remains high. This simultaneously creates a shortage and pushes prices upward; option B wrongly assumes that high prices automatically generate enough new housing.

questions.stem: A city proposes installing green roofs on old public housing blocks. Which option best explains the feature’s mechanism, sustainability pillar and limitation?
options: Vegetation absorbs less heat and provides evaporative cooling, advancing environmental sustainability, but maintenance is expensive on old buildings.
Green roofs absorb sunlight and improve air quality, advancing social sustainability, but they reduce residents’ quality of life.
Green roofs conserve natural resources and create jobs, advancing economic sustainability, but they may limit community participation.
Green roofs control pollution and protect ecosystems, advancing environmental sustainability, but they provide little equity or fairness.
questions.explanation: Green roofs reduce the urban heat island effect because vegetation absorbs less heat than concrete and provides evaporative cooling, supporting environmental sustainability; however, they can be expensive to maintain on old buildings. Option B is wrong because the main mechanism and stated pillar do not match.

questions.stem: A neighbourhood invites residents to vote on a proposed environmental improvement project. Which sustainability benefit is most directly demonstrated?
options: Greater community participation and more equitable decision-making, advancing social sustainability.
More efficient resource use and stronger economic growth, advancing economic sustainability.
Better pollution control and ecosystem protection, advancing environmental sustainability.
Improved job creation and higher household income, advancing economic sustainability.
questions.explanation: Allowing residents to participate in decisions promotes equity and fairness, which are key aspects of social sustainability. Option B is the main distractor because the scenario demonstrates participation and fairness, not efficient resource use or economic growth.

questions.stem: Hong Kong imports electricity from the Mainland. Which statement gives the most balanced evaluation of this energy strategy?
options: It diversifies supply and can lower costs and local emissions, but dependence on the Mainland creates a vulnerability.
It removes dependence on external energy because Hong Kong controls all Mainland generating facilities.
It is sustainable only if Hong Kong stops relying on imported fossil fuels from the Mainland.
It lowers local emissions but always raises electricity prices because transmission infrastructure is costly.
questions.explanation: Importing Mainland electricity diversifies energy sources and can lower costs and local emissions, but it creates dependency. B is wrong because importing electricity does not remove external dependence or give Hong Kong control over Mainland facilities.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest justification for using the I·PARK1 waste-to-energy facility in land-scarce Hong Kong?
options: It moves waste up the hierarchy: incineration reduces volume and recovers energy when landfill space cannot expand.
It makes landfill extension unnecessary because incineration can recycle all materials into new products.
It removes the need for source separation because mixed waste can be converted into usable materials.
It eliminates all air pollution and ash disposal problems through energy recovery.
questions.explanation: Because disposal land cannot expand, incineration’s volume reduction and energy recovery help Hong Kong move up the waste hierarchy. D is wrong because emissions-control costs, ash disposal and public acceptance remain important limitations.

questions.stem: A city installs recycling bins, but residents continue to litter rather than recycle. Which evaluation best explains the weakness of this strategy?
options: The government has provided facilities without securing community participation; provision alone does not create recycling habits.
The city should use zoning to separate residential and industrial land and anticipate environmental problems before development.
The city should control building height and density to protect light and ventilation near recycling facilities.
The city should rely on education alone, because awareness campaigns always produce rapid and certain changes in behaviour.
questions.explanation: Provision without participation can fail: recycling bins are ineffective if residents lack the habits and willingness to use them. Option D is incorrect because education is slow and uncertain, and works only where suitable alternatives exist.

questions.stem: Which option best evaluates green belts as a planning strategy for a sustainable, land-scarce, high-density city?
options: They permanently cap urban sprawl and protect recreational or ecological space, but may raise land prices and push development beyond the boundary.
They separate residential and industrial land, preventing incompatible uses before they arise, but may create long commutes.
They control building height and density, protecting light and ventilation, but may worsen overcrowding.
They provide land for public consultation and NGO programmes, improving legitimacy but requiring sustained community participation.
questions.explanation: Green belts reserve land from development, permanently limiting urban sprawl and protecting open space. Their main limitation is that they may increase land prices inside the boundary and encourage development further away; option B describes zoning.

questions.stem: A Hong Kong waste charge aims to reduce rubbish. Which judgement best explains why its sustainability cannot be judged by environmental benefits alone?
options: It is sustainable if the government can finance waste collection and has enough vehicles to enforce the charge.
It is sustainable because economic costs occur now, while environmental benefits will be larger in the future.
It is sustainable only if short-term economic and social costs are acceptable and implementation is feasible, while delayed environmental benefits justify the policy.
It is sustainable if most residents accept the charge, regardless of its costs and environmental effectiveness.
questions.explanation: A sustainable measure must be feasible and create an acceptable balance between present costs and longer-term benefits. Option B addresses delayed benefits but ignores whether the costs are acceptable and whether the policy can be implemented effectively.

questions.stem: Which explanation best applies the free-rider idea to Hong Kong's promotion of household recycling?
options: Residents may recycle because they expect direct cash rebates rather than because they understand the environmental benefits.
Some residents may benefit from reduced landfill use while avoiding the inconvenience and costs of recycling.
Publicity can improve recycling only if every household has convenient access to recycling facilities.
Residents may support recycling in principle but reject the inconvenience of sorting materials at home.
questions.explanation: The free-rider problem occurs when people enjoy environmental benefits without bearing the associated costs. Option D describes an acceptance problem, but it does not explain why some residents benefit from others' recycling efforts.

questions.stem: A farmer in a semi-arid region has abundant sunlight and capital for machinery, but crop yields remain low. Which analysis correctly distinguishes the production systems and identifies the binding constraint?
options: Sunlight is a biological input; machinery is an economic capital input; irrigation water is likely the binding constraint.
Sunlight is an economic input; machinery is a biological input; fertile soil is the binding constraint.
Land rent is a biological input; irrigation water is an economic input; labour costs are the binding constraint.
Machinery and fertiliser are biological inputs; management skill is an economic input; sunlight is the binding constraint.
questions.explanation: Sunlight and water are biological inputs, whereas machinery, rent and paid labour belong to the economic system. In a semi-arid region, deficient water is likely to limit yield; adding capital alone cannot overcome this constraint.

questions.stem: Which interpretation best reflects the spectrum of farming types and their relationship with food security?
options: Subsistence farming has little surplus, while commercial farming can use storage and market access to reduce famine risk; organic farming is defined by methods, not scale.
Subsistence farming has a large surplus, while commercial farming relies mainly on hired labour; organic farming is always a smallholding.
Subsistence and commercial farming differ only in their use of organic methods; organic farming always has higher yields than commercial farming.
Commercial farming has little surplus and high famine risk; subsistence farming is more food-secure because it is labour-intensive.
questions.explanation: Subsistence farming’s thin surplus leaves it vulnerable when one season fails, whereas commercial farming can buffer volatility through storage and market access. Organic farming concerns natural methods and can operate at either a small or large scale, so it is not simply a stage between subsistence and commercial farming.

questions.stem: During a Sahel drought, grain is available in some surplus-producing areas, yet remote households go hungry. Which explanation best distinguishes famine from drought?
options: Inadequate roads and storage prevented food from reaching deficit areas, so production and access both failed.
Rainfall fell below 100 mm, making crop production impossible throughout the entire Sahel.
High temperatures increased evapotranspiration, reducing the moisture available to rain-fed crops.
Rapid population growth increased demand, so surplus had to be distributed more efficiently.
questions.explanation: Drought is the climatic hazard, whereas famine is a food-system failure. Even if total production remains adequate, weak transport and storage can prevent food from reaching hungry people. C explains the physical hazard but not why hunger occurs where surplus food exists.

questions.stem: Which explanation best shows why the Sahel is marginal, how degradation strengthens drought, and why famine can follow?
options: Immediately south of the Sahara, 100–400 mm rainfall is unreliable; high evapotranspiration, water scarcity and soil degradation from overgrazing and deforestation reduce yields.
The Sahel is a true desert: rainfall is consistently scarce, and drought is its only natural cause of food insecurity.
Its high rainfall makes farming stable; famine occurs only because population growth outpaces food production.
Its soils are naturally infertile, while rainfall, temperature and land management have no significant influence.
questions.explanation: The Sahel lies at the desert–savanna margin, where low, variable rainfall and high evapotranspiration already limit rain-fed farming. Overgrazing and deforestation expose soil, accelerating erosion, nutrient depletion and desertification, so drought can cause crop failure and famine. B is wrong because the Sahel is a semi-arid marginal belt, not a true desert.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for both the high productivity of Southern Californian agriculture and its main sustainability risks?
options: Mediterranean sunshine supports high yields, but imported, over-allocated river water and irrigation-induced salinisation constrain farming.
Fertile alluvial soils and reliable summer rainfall remove the need for irrigation, although drought may occasionally reduce output.
Low humidity eliminates crop disease, so high sunshine alone removes the region’s binding constraint of water supply.
Controlled-environment growing replaces the Colorado River, allowing agriculture to expand without importing water or raising salinity.
questions.explanation: Dry, sunny summers favour high yields, but water must be imported from the over-allocated Colorado River. Irrigation raises the water table; evaporation leaves salts in the topsoil, causing osmotic damage and reducing yields. B is wrong because Southern California has dry summers and depends on irrigation.

questions.stem: Which set of human factors best explains how Southern California turns its physical advantages into highly productive farming?
options: Mechanisation and monitoring raise output; drip and sprinkler systems apply water precisely; capital, government support and research reinforce these gains.
Traditional hand labour substitutes for machinery, while seasonal rainfall removes the need for costly irrigation infrastructure and research.
Capital funds irrigation and technology, but government regulation and research are unnecessary because alluvial soils naturally suit every crop.
Research institutions develop heat- and disease-resistant varieties, but advanced technology and infrastructure add little to output.
questions.explanation: Advanced technology raises yields per hectare and worker, while precise irrigation converts the region’s physical advantages into production. Capital funds equipment and marketing, government provides infrastructure and subsidies, and research develops suitable varieties and techniques. B is wrong because mechanisation, irrigation and research are central to productivity.

questions.stem: A region produces enough food, but many people cannot buy it, move it, or receive aid; widespread hunger and deaths occur. Which option best describes this situation using the working definition of famine?
options: A severe shortage of accessible food causing widespread hunger and death
A temporary fall in total food output without widespread hunger or death
A natural hazard such as drought, regardless of access or distribution
A localized disruption to food prices in a generally well-fed region
questions.explanation: Famine is a severe shortage of food causing widespread hunger and death, and food access and distribution are as important as total production. Option C confuses a natural hazard with famine; a hazard becomes famine when the food system cannot respond.

questions.stem: Drought reduces rain-fed harvests in the Sahel. Which option best shows human root causes turning this natural trigger into famine?
options: Poor roads delay food aid, while poverty prevents households from buying substitute food
Reduced harvests alone prove famine because total production matters more than food access
Food aid reaches the Sahel, but export policies prevent farmers from selling surplus crops
Population growth is the natural trigger, while rainfall variability is a human root cause
questions.explanation: Drought is the natural trigger because it reduces harvests, while poor roads and poverty prevent an effective response, turning the shortfall into famine. Option B wrongly suggests that reduced production alone is sufficient and ignores access and distribution.

questions.stem: A Sahel government wants to reduce repeated famine risk while avoiding dependence on emergency relief. Which measure best serves this long-term aim?
options: Irrigation: supplying reliable water removes a production constraint, allowing more consistent harvests.
Food imports: raising national food availability quickly will strengthen local agricultural production.
Price controls: keeping food prices low will encourage farmers to invest and increase supply.
Medical care: treating malnutrition and disease will remove the underlying causes of famine.
questions.explanation: Irrigation is a long-term development measure because it removes a water constraint and supports more reliable local production. Food imports provide short-term availability but do not improve local production, while medical care mainly reduces famine mortality.

questions.stem: Which evaluation of GM crops as a solution to famine is most defensible?
options: GM crops should be rejected because their long-term health effects are proven harmful and farmers will become dependent on corporations.
GM crops can improve yields and nutritional quality, but may not solve famine alone because conflict, purchasing power and access remain concerns.
GM crops will solve famine because higher yields automatically improve food access and reduce prices for poor households.
GM crops are unnecessary because traditional seeds and irrigation can always provide sufficient food without environmental or corporate risks.
questions.explanation: B balances potential benefits, such as higher effective yields and improved nutrition, with limitations involving access and the unresolved effects of corporate dependency and environmental risk. C is too absolute because higher yields do not automatically guarantee that vulnerable people can obtain food.

questions.stem: A farm proposes crop rotation, drip irrigation and agroforestry. Which option best evaluates the proposal using the three pillars of sustainable agriculture?
options: Rotation reduces fertiliser use; drip irrigation conserves water; agroforestry supports ecosystems and communities, but costs and market returns must remain affordable.
Crop rotation conserves soil, so fertiliser costs and environmental damage fall; the other practices are unnecessary if yields remain high.
Drip irrigation protects water supplies, while agroforestry raises output; therefore, environmental gains alone demonstrate sustainability.
Agroforestry supports biodiversity and rural communities, so higher short-term costs are justified even if the farm cannot cover them.
questions.explanation: A links each practice to a mechanism and then considers the economic requirement of affordability alongside environmental and social benefits. B wrongly assumes that one beneficial practice makes the other measures unnecessary.

questions.stem: The table shows Australia has 12.3 million ha of organic land (2.8%), Italy 1.1 million ha (9.0%) and China 2.3 million ha (0.4%). Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Australia leads in absolute area; Italy leads in share; higher-income countries generally have higher shares, consistent with premiums or regulation but not proving causation.
Australia leads in organic share, while Italy has the largest organic area because Italian farms are generally smaller.
China has a high organic share, and its lower income per person proves that consumer premiums drive organic adoption.
Australia’s large area shows a high share of organic farming, while Italy’s much smaller area indicates limited adoption.
questions.explanation: A correctly distinguishes absolute area from percentage share and treats the relationship with income as correlation rather than proof of causation. B confuses area with share, which is a common error when reading the table.

questions.stem: Which climatic conditions are characteristic of the tropical rainforest biome?
options: Temperatures of 25–27°C throughout the year, annual rainfall of 2,000–4,000 mm and humidity above 80%
Temperatures of 15–20°C throughout the year, annual rainfall of 500–1,000 mm and humidity around 50%
Temperatures of 25–27°C throughout the year, annual rainfall of 500–1,000 mm and humidity above 80%
Temperatures of 20–25°C with marked seasonal changes, annual rainfall of 1,500–2,500 mm and humidity of 60–70%
questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests have consistently high temperatures, very high annual rainfall and humidity above 80%. Option C is a plausible distractor because it has the correct heat and humidity, but its annual rainfall is too low for the tropical rainforest biome.

questions.stem: Which description best fits the vegetation of a tropical rainforest?
options: A well-developed upper canopy and a wide variety of species
An open upper layer dominated by a few widespread species
A sparse lower layer with very little species variety
A single-storey vegetation layer with highly specialised species
questions.explanation: A canopy is the upper layer of forest, and tropical rainforests are noted for their high biodiversity, meaning a wide variety of species. Option B is incorrect because the combination of an open upper layer and very low species variety does not characterise tropical rainforests.

questions.stem: A vegetation survey finds a tree at 12 metres in the lower canopy. Which description best matches this layer?
options: Shade-tolerant trees and climbing plants are characteristic.
Tallest trees dominate, forming 3–5% of the forest.
Dense, continuous vegetation carries out 90% of photosynthesis.
Sparse vegetation grows in darkness with little sunlight.
questions.explanation: The lower canopy, 10–20 metres above ground, contains shade-tolerant trees and climbing plants. Option C describes the upper canopy, while the sparse vegetation and limited sunlight in option D characterize the ground layer below 10 metres.

questions.stem: Which option correctly describes the emergent layer of a rainforest?
options: It reaches 35–45 metres and contains about 3–5% of the forest’s trees.
It forms dense, continuous cover at 30–35 metres and carries out 90% of photosynthesis.
It contains large tree crowns at 20–30 metres, with epiphytes present.
It has shade-tolerant trees and climbing plants at 10–20 metres.
questions.explanation: The emergent layer contains the tallest trees, reaching 35–45 metres, and only 3–5% of the forest. Option B describes the upper canopy, which forms dense cover and carries out 90% of photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes nutrient storage and recycling in a tropical rainforest?
options: Most nutrients are stored in the soil and remain there for many years.
Most nutrients are stored in biomass and efficiently recycled through rapid uptake and decomposition.
Most nutrients are stored in litter and are returned slowly by rock weathering.
Nutrients mainly enter through harvesting and leave through surface runoff.
questions.explanation: About 70–80% of nutrients are stored in biomass, compared with 15–25% in soil. Rapid root absorption, fast decomposition and efficient recycling maintain this store. Option A is wrong because the soil contains much less of the rainforest’s nutrients.

questions.stem: Why can the nutrient cycle of a tropical rainforest become fragile after deforestation?
options: Nutrients wash away less because the exposed forest floor has no vegetation.
Nutrient uptake and storage decline as trees are removed, increasing losses through leaching and runoff.
Deforestation increases nitrogen fixation, adding nutrients to the soil.
Fallen biomass compensates for removed trees by increasing nutrient uptake.
questions.explanation: The rapid nutrient cycle depends heavily on trees for nutrient uptake and storage. Clearing them reduces biomass and allows nutrients to be lost through leaching and runoff. Option A is wrong because exposed soil is more susceptible to nutrient loss, not less.

questions.stem: According to the 2025 case, which two factors were the main drivers of primary-forest loss in Bolivia?
options: Soy cultivation and agricultural expansion
Shifting cultivation and charcoal production
Palm-oil plantations and mining
Oil-palm conversion of indigenous land
questions.explanation: The Bolivia case identifies agriculture and the Santa Cruz soy frontier as the main drivers. Shifting cultivation and charcoal production were linked mainly to DR Congo, while palm oil and mining were associated with Indonesia.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for Indonesia's 14% year-on-year increase in primary-forest loss in 2025?
options: Expansion of soy farms in Bolivia
Increased shifting cultivation in DR Congo
Palm-oil plantations and mining activities
Intensification of boreal forest fires in Canada
questions.explanation: The Indonesia case states that palm oil and mining remained key drivers of forest clearance. The other options describe drivers associated with different locations and do not explain Indonesia's increase.

questions.stem: Which option correctly links the hydrological and climatic effects of deforestation?
options: Less infiltration and more runoff increase flooding; less sequestration raises atmospheric CO₂ and global warming.
More infiltration and less runoff reduce flooding; less sequestration lowers atmospheric CO₂ and global warming.
Less infiltration and less runoff increase flooding; greater sequestration lowers atmospheric CO₂ and global warming.
More infiltration and more runoff reduce flooding; greater sequestration raises atmospheric CO₂ and global warming.
questions.explanation: Deforestation reduces infiltration and increases runoff, raising flood risk, while reduced carbon sequestration increases atmospheric CO₂ and contributes to global warming. C is wrong because runoff increases and carbon sequestration decreases.

questions.stem: Which sequence best explains how deforestation disrupts the nutrient cycle and reduces soil fertility?
options: Less biomass, more leaching and erosion, and greater runoff reduce nutrient retention.
More biomass and slower runoff increase nutrient storage, reversing soil decline.
Greater infiltration and faster decomposition return minerals to the soil more efficiently.
Laterite formation supplies nutrients, so soil fertility rises as forest cover is removed.
questions.explanation: Removing trees reduces biomass storage and soil protection, while nutrients are leached away and water runs off, causing soil fertility to decline. B is wrong because deforestation reduces biomass and accelerates rather than slows runoff.

questions.stem: In 2025, DR Congo lost 560,000 ha of primary forest, while Indonesia lost 433,751 ha. Which comparison of scale and causes is supported?
options: DR Congo had the larger loss, while Indonesia’s deforestation was driven only by palm-oil plantations.
