B It reduces pollution because cultural districts automatically attract electric transport and replace all nearby industrial activities.
C It mainly improves environmental sustainability because regenerating and re-imaging a district do not affect its economy or social life.
D It guarantees equity and fairness because adaptive reuse automatically provides affordable housing for all former industrial workers.
questions.explanation: Adaptive reuse conserves resources, while a cultural and creative district can support economic growth and job creation; community participation and equitable access strengthen social sustainability. B is wrong because pollution reduction is not automatic merely because a district has been re-imaged as cultural.

questions.stem: A Hong Kong developer is considering installing green roofs on an old commercial building. Which option best explains the measure, its mechanism, the sustainability pillar advanced and a limitation?
options: Vegetation provides shade and evaporative cooling, reducing the urban heat island effect; it advances environmental sustainability, but maintenance is expensive on old buildings.
Vegetation reduces cooling demand and supports economic sustainability, although installing green roofs requires no capital on existing buildings.
Plants collect rainwater for nearby communities, advancing social sustainability, although urban heat may intensify beneath them.
Green roofs replace natural habitats and protect ecosystems, but they cannot reduce the temperatures of surrounding buildings.
questions.explanation: Green roofs reduce the urban heat island effect through shade and evaporative cooling, advancing environmental sustainability, but maintenance can be expensive on old buildings. B wrongly classifies the main benefit under economic sustainability and removes the limitation.
questions.subtopic_title: The price of developing a sustainable city

questions.stem: Which measure most directly demonstrates social sustainability when a new sustainable-city district is planned in Hong Kong?
options: Residents join neighbourhood meetings and help determine priorities for community facilities.
Engineers recycle construction waste to conserve natural resources and reduce pollution.
Training programmes create jobs for local residents and support economic growth.
The council installs pollution-control equipment to protect ecosystems near the district.
questions.explanation: A reflects community participation, a key feature of social sustainability, and can promote equity and quality of life. B and D mainly demonstrate environmental sustainability, while C mainly demonstrates economic sustainability.
questions.subtopic_title: The price of developing a sustainable city

questions.stem: Region P produces 12 million tonnes of food for 12 million residents. However, some residents cannot afford food or reach distribution channels. Which statement best applies the definition of famine?
options: Famine in P would necessarily indicate that total production is below demand.
Famine can occur where food is produced but people cannot buy, move or receive it.
Equal total production and population guarantee that everyone receives adequate food.
The population size alone proves that P's food supply is adequate.
questions.explanation: Famine concerns access to and distribution of food, not only total production. Option A is wrong because insufficient total production is not necessary for famine where people cannot obtain the food produced.
questions.subtopic_title: Global patterns of food production, consumption and trade

questions.stem: Table 1 shows Region A has 10 million residents and produces 30 million tonnes of food; Region B has 30 million residents and also produces 30 million tonnes. Which statement is best justified?
options: A has higher production per person, but consumption also depends on imports and access to food.
Both regions must have identical food consumption because their total production is identical.
A necessarily consumes more food per person because its production per person is higher.
B must have adequate food supplies because its total production equals Region A's.
questions.explanation: Region A produces 3 tonnes per resident, compared with 1 tonne in Region B, but production does not directly establish consumption. Option C is wrong because residents may be unable to buy or receive the food produced.
questions.subtopic_title: Global patterns of food production, consumption and trade

questions.stem: An irrigated farm has declining yields, and salt has accumulated near the surface after repeated over-irrigation. Which process is responsible?
options: Saline soil formation caused naturally by hot, dry, low-rainfall conditions.
Salinisation caused by irrigation misuse raising the water table and accumulating salts.
Soil erosion caused by floods washing away fertile topsoil.
Chemical pollution caused by agrochemical runoff entering nearby watercourses.
questions.explanation: Over-irrigation raises the water table, allowing capillary action to bring salts to the surface, so this is human-induced salinisation. Option A is incorrect because naturally saline soil results from hot, dry and low-rainfall conditions, not irrigation misuse.
questions.subtopic_title: Consequences of misuse and overuse of agricultural technology

questions.stem: A farm wants to reduce agrochemical runoff into watercourses and conserve biodiversity while remaining profitable, treating workers fairly and benefiting the community. Which approach best reflects sustainable agriculture?
options: Conserve soil, water and biodiversity, reduce pollution, remain profitable, and support fair labour and the community.
Conserve soil and biodiversity only, even if the farm can no longer cover its operating costs.
Remain profitable through intensive production, even if chemical runoff increases and ecosystems are damaged.
Ensure food security and fair labour, even if pollution reduction raises costs beyond what the farm can afford.
questions.explanation: Option A balances the environmental, economic and social pillars of sustainable agriculture. Option B fails the economic pillar because a farm unable to cover its costs will not persist, while Option C sacrifices environmental sustainability.
questions.subtopic_title: Consequences of misuse and overuse of agricultural technology

questions.stem: A farm alternates different crop species between seasons. Which explanation best describes how crop rotation contributes to sustainable agriculture?
options: It maintains soil nutrients and breaks pest and disease cycles, reducing fertiliser and pesticide needs.
It supplies water directly to roots, minimising evaporation during dry periods.
It integrates trees with crops to provide shade, shelter and several sources of income.
It stores wet-season water for use during the dry season.
questions.explanation: Different crop species draw on different nutrients and host different pests, so rotation maintains soil fertility and interrupts pest and disease cycles. Option C describes agroforestry, while B and D describe water-management methods rather than crop rotation.
questions.subtopic_title: Multiple cropping, water conservation and soil conservation

questions.stem: A farm in a water-scarce region wants to reduce irrigation water loss while continuing to grow crops. Which measure directly addresses this objective, and how?
options: Use drip irrigation to deliver water directly to roots with minimal evaporation.
Harvest rainwater so that wet-season water can be stored for the dry season.
Recycle treated wastewater to reduce the farm's demand on freshwater supplies.
Rotate crops to maintain soil nutrients and interrupt pest cycles.
questions.explanation: Drip irrigation directly reduces water loss by delivering water to roots with minimal evaporation. Rainwater harvesting and wastewater recycling improve water availability, but they do not directly minimise evaporation during irrigation.
questions.subtopic_title: Multiple cropping, water conservation and soil conservation

questions.stem: Large-scale clearance of the tree canopy occurs on a Hong Kong farm. Which sequence most directly indicates that the ecosystem’s balance has been disturbed?
options: Species habitat loss → extinction risk → ecosystem disruption
Less infiltration → more runoff → flooding
Fertility decline → laterite formation → erosion
Less carbon sequestration → global warming → more atmospheric CO₂
questions.explanation: Habitat loss and greater extinction risk directly weaken biodiversity, disrupting the ecosystem’s balance. Option B is also associated with canopy loss, but it describes a hydrological response rather than ecological equilibrium.
questions.subtopic_title: Abiotic and biotic components, energy flow and ecological equilibrium

questions.stem: In an agricultural ecosystem, sunlight powers photosynthesis, while water and soil nutrients support crop growth. Which statement correctly describes the link between abiotic and biotic components?
options: Sunlight is an abiotic energy source used by crops through photosynthesis
Soil is a biotic component because it supplies nutrients to plants
Water transfers sunlight directly to plants during photosynthesis
Labour is the main abiotic source of energy for photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Sunlight is a non-living energy source, while crops are living components that use it in photosynthesis. Option C confuses water’s role in plant growth with the transfer of solar energy.
questions.subtopic_title: Abiotic and biotic components, energy flow and ecological equilibrium

questions.stem: The table shows the relationship between deforestation rate and carbon surplus. Which conclusion is most consistent with the data and the rainforest carbon cycle?
options: A higher deforestation rate is associated with a larger carbon surplus because forest clearing reduces CO2 absorption.
A higher deforestation rate is associated with a smaller carbon surplus because cleared forests release less carbon.
Deforestation rate and carbon surplus have no relationship because forests do not absorb atmospheric carbon.
A lower deforestation rate is associated with a larger carbon surplus because remaining forests absorb more CO2.
questions.explanation: The table directly links a higher deforestation rate with a larger carbon surplus. Clearing forests reduces carbon sequestration and CO2 absorption, while option B incorrectly reverses this relationship.
questions.subtopic_title: Global distribution and the rate of deforestation

questions.stem: Which statement is correctly supported by the 2025 updates on tropical rainforest regions?
options: Brazilian Amazon deforestation increased overall, and Mato Grosso was the only state where the rate rose.
Bolivia experienced the highest per-area primary-forest loss in the Amazon basin, mainly because of agriculture and soy expansion.
Indonesia's primary-forest loss continued the decade-long decline, with palm oil and mining becoming less important.
DR Congo's forest loss was mainly caused by oil-palm planting and large-scale mining rather than shifting cultivation and charcoal production.
questions.explanation: The updates identify Bolivia's approximately 20% share of non-fire primary-forest loss, driven mainly by agriculture and the Santa Cruz soy frontier. Option D incorrectly identifies the main causes of DR Congo's loss, while the Brazilian and Indonesian trends in A and C are also reversed.
questions.subtopic_title: Global distribution and the rate of deforestation

questions.stem: In Sarawak, Penan and Kenyah communities sued over 54,478 ha of native customary land allegedly cleared for oil-palm planting. Which conflict is best illustrated?
options: Indigenous land rights versus private developers’ agricultural expansion
Local dwellers’ hunting needs versus government forest conservation policies
Environmentalists’ tourism plans versus indigenous shifting cultivation
Government officials’ mining interests versus private developers’ biofuel projects
questions.explanation: The Penan and Kenyah were defending their customary land rights, while oil-palm developers sought to convert forest land for agriculture. The conflict therefore centred on indigenous land ownership and developers’ commercial interests, not hunting, tourism or mining.
questions.subtopic_title: Roles of different parties and conflicts of interest

questions.stem: Which combination best represents the roles of the main stakeholders in protecting rainforest resources while meeting local needs?
options: Officials enforce policies; developers follow rules; environmentalists advocate protection; local dwellers use alternative livelihoods
Officials permit unrestricted clearance; developers ignore regulations; environmentalists expand farming; local dwellers reject conservation
Officials replace forests with plantations; developers manage protected areas; environmentalists promote clearance; local dwellers rely only on hunting
Officials fund all deforestation; developers eliminate protected areas; environmentalists oppose all farming; local dwellers avoid the forest
questions.explanation: This combination assigns complementary roles: officials enforce conservation policies, developers comply with restrictions, environmentalists advocate protection, and local dwellers reduce dependence on forest resources through alternative livelihoods. The other options assign roles that intensify deforestation rather than balance protection with local needs.
questions.subtopic_title: Roles of different parties and conflicts of interest

questions.stem: In the Amazon Basin, logging roads open up forest for further clearance. Which official measure most directly addresses the destruction caused by timber extraction?
options: Regulation on logging activities
Afforestation
Setting up national parks and natural reserves
Land reform
questions.explanation: Regulation on logging activities directly controls timber extraction and can reduce forest clearance. Protected areas and land reform also conserve forests, but they do not directly regulate logging.
questions.subtopic_title: Afforestation, logging regulation, national parks and natural reserves

questions.stem: China’s 2025 programme greened 8.47 million ha of land, including 3.56 million ha through afforestation. Which official measure is best illustrated by planting trees on suitable land?
options: Setting up national parks and natural reserves
Regulation on logging activities
Land reform
Afforestation
questions.explanation: Afforestation is the planting of trees to increase forest cover, matching the land-greening programme. National parks and natural reserves involve designating protected areas rather than primarily planting trees.
questions.subtopic_title: Afforestation, logging regulation, national parks and natural reserves

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes weather from climate?
options: Weather describes atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time, while climate describes long-term patterns of weather.
Weather is the long-term average of atmospheric conditions, while climate describes conditions on a particular day.
Weather and climate both refer only to changes in average global temperature over several decades.
Weather describes long-term rainfall patterns, while climate describes temperature at a particular place and time.
questions.explanation: Weather concerns atmospheric conditions at a particular place and time, whereas climate concerns long-term weather patterns. Option B reverses these definitions by describing climate as short-term.
questions.subtopic_title: Weather versus climate, and climate at local, national and global scale

questions.stem: Which option correctly matches climate-related activities with local, national and global scales?
options: Local: assessing long-term climate patterns in a Hong Kong district; national: setting an NDC; global: participating in IPCC or COP work.
Local: negotiating an NDC; national: recording weather in a Hong Kong district; global: preparing a local flood warning.
Local: assessing global temperatures for an IPCC report; national: examining rainfall in a district; global: issuing a local heat warning.
Local: agreeing targets under an NDC; national: coordinating COP negotiations; global: recording weather in Hong Kong.
questions.explanation: A small-area study of long-term patterns is local, an NDC is determined nationally, and IPCC and COP operate globally. Option C incorrectly presents an IPCC assessment of global temperatures as a national activity.
questions.subtopic_title: Weather versus climate, and climate at local, national and global scale

questions.stem: Which explanation correctly distinguishes the natural greenhouse effect from the enhanced greenhouse effect associated with global warming?
options: A Natural greenhouse gases keep Earth warm, while additional greenhouse gases from human activities trap more heat and raise global temperatures.
B Human greenhouse-gas emissions create the natural greenhouse effect, while changes in hot and cold days create the enhanced greenhouse effect.
C Both effects arise from the same natural gases, but only the natural greenhouse effect traps heat and warms Earth.
D The natural greenhouse effect warms Earth from −18°C to +15°C, but human activities reduce the heat trapped by greenhouse gases.
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect involves gases such as CO₂, H₂O, CH₄ and N₂O keeping Earth warm. Human activities add more greenhouse gases, trapping more heat and causing global temperatures to rise; B wrongly treats changes in hot and cold days as a cause.
questions.subtopic_title: Natural versus human causes, and the irreversible-trend debate

questions.stem: Which option best evaluates the evidence for global warming while presenting the debate over whether it is a long-term fluctuation or an irreversible trend?
options: A The 1.1°C rise, warmest last decade, more hot days and fewer cold days support a warming trend; however, an opposing view treats this as a long-term fluctuation.
B The recorded warming proves that temperatures only fluctuate and provides no support for the view that warming represents an irreversible trend.
C Changes in hot and cold days show that warming is only a fluctuation, so the 1.1°C rise cannot be evidence of a warming trend.
D The temperature record supports only the irreversible-trend argument because climate change involves long-term changes in weather patterns.
questions.explanation: The temperature rise, warmest decade and changing frequency of hot and cold days support an ongoing warming trend, while the opposing argument interprets it as a long-term fluctuation. B is wrong because the recorded evidence supports a warming trend rather than showing only fluctuating temperatures.
questions.subtopic_title: Natural versus human causes, and the irreversible-trend debate

questions.stem: Which set of human activities enhances the greenhouse effect?
options: Deforestation, burning fossil fuels, garbage burning and emission of CFCs
Deforestation, burning fossil fuels, garbage burning and increased use of renewable energy
Deforestation, burning fossil fuels, planting trees and emission of CFCs
Deforestation, natural decomposition of plant matter, garbage burning and emission of CFCs
questions.explanation: The listed activities increase greenhouse gases, causing more heat to be trapped and global temperatures to rise. Option B is incorrect because increased use of renewable energy is a mitigation measure rather than an activity that enhances the greenhouse effect.
questions.subtopic_title: Garbage burning and other named human activities

questions.stem: Which human activity is correctly matched with the greenhouse gas that it mainly increases?
options: Burning fossil fuels — carbon dioxide
Livestock farming — nitrous oxide
Use of fertilisers — methane
Emission of CFCs — nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, adding to the greenhouse effect by increasing the amount of heat trapped. Option D is incorrect because CFCs are themselves greenhouse gases, not nitrous oxide.
questions.subtopic_title: Garbage burning and other named human activities

questions.stem: Which feature of urban development in Hong Kong most directly contributes to the urban heat island effect?
options: Extensive paved surfaces replacing vegetation
More high-rise buildings increasing sea-breeze penetration
Greater use of reflective roofs in new districts
Construction of reservoirs within urban areas
questions.explanation: Paved and built-up surfaces absorb and store heat, while vegetation loss reduces cooling by evapotranspiration. Sea breezes normally cool urban areas, so option B would weaken rather than strengthen the heat island effect.
questions.subtopic_title: Urban climate: the heat island effect and microclimate

questions.stem: Which combination best describes the likely effects of an urban heat island in a Hong Kong city district?
options: Higher temperature, increased convective rainfall and greater local pollutant concentrations
Lower temperature, reduced rainfall and cleaner air
Higher temperature, lower rainfall and more atmospheric oxygen
Little temperature variation, more fog and lower humidity
questions.explanation: Urban heating promotes rising air and convection, potentially increasing summer rainfall, while traffic emissions and poor dispersion can raise local pollutant concentrations. Option B is incorrect because urban surfaces generally warm the surrounding air rather than cool it.
questions.subtopic_title: Urban climate: the heat island effect and microclimate

questions.stem: Which sequence best explains the main sea-level threat faced by residents of a low-lying Hong Kong coastal community?
options: Glacier melt and thermal expansion → sea-level rise → more frequent coastal flooding
Glacier melt and thermal expansion → sea-level rise → fewer coastal floods
Ocean warming → sea-level rise → more predictable farming gains
Glacier growth and thermal contraction → sea-level rise → lower flood frequency
questions.explanation: Melting glaciers and thermal expansion raise sea levels, increasing coastal flooding risk for low-lying communities. Option B is wrong because sea-level rise makes flooding more frequent, not less frequent.
questions.subtopic_title: Winners and losers of climate change

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the mixed consequences of global warming for different people?
options: Health risks may increase for some people, new farming opportunities may benefit others, and climatic prediction may become more difficult
Health risks may increase for most people, new farming opportunities may benefit everyone, and climatic prediction may become easier
Health risks may decline for some people, new farming opportunities may benefit others, and climatic prediction may become easier
Health risks may increase for some people, new farming opportunities may benefit others, and climatic prediction may become more reliable
questions.explanation: Global warming can create losers through increased health risks and possible winners through new farming opportunities, while long-term weather-pattern changes make climatic prediction more difficult. Option D is wrong because these changes do not generally make climatic prediction more reliable.
questions.subtopic_title: Winners and losers of climate change

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement (2015) was signed by 196 countries and aimed to limit warming to 1.5–2°C. Which feature best shows the complexity of reaching a global agreement?
options: NDCs allow countries to determine their own contributions, so different national priorities may complicate agreement.
A single mandatory target applies to every country, removing conflicts over national contributions.
Only countries facing the greatest climate risks are included in the agreement.
The agreement relies on a global emissions target, so countries have no role in setting contributions.
questions.explanation: NDCs are nationally determined contributions, allowing different national circumstances and priorities to shape commitments. This can make agreement on the common 1.5–2°C goal difficult, unlike distractor B, which wrongly suggests that every country has an identical mandatory target.
questions.subtopic_title: Conflicting views and roles of key players

questions.stem: Which comparison correctly shows how the roles of countries differed between the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement?
options: Kyoto focused on emissions reductions by developed countries; Paris involved 196 countries through NDCs.
Kyoto involved 196 countries; Paris focused only on emissions reductions by developed countries.
Kyoto required NDCs from all countries; Paris required only developed countries to reduce emissions.
Both agreements placed binding reduction responsibilities on all countries in the same way.
questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol was the first binding agreement and placed reduction requirements on developed countries. The Paris Agreement involved 196 countries and used NDCs, so distractor B reverses the roles of the two agreements.
questions.subtopic_title: Conflicting views and roles of key players

questions.stem: A student must overlay Hong Kong’s urban development map on a relief map to demonstrate how development has modified the landscape. Which method would provide the clearest valid comparison?
options: Overlay the urban-development layer semi-transparently on relief shading, align both maps, and examine where built-up areas coincide with valleys and slopes.
Place the maps side by side and compare the locations of towns with named mountains without matching their positions.
Use building density alone to reconstruct the relief, assuming that denser areas indicate steeper slopes.
Overlay a geological map on the relief map and use fault locations to infer all urban development.
questions.explanation: An aligned, semi-transparent overlay directly shows the spatial relationship between urban development and the pre-existing relief. A geological map may identify faults, but it cannot by itself show where and how urban development modified the landscape.
questions.subtopic_title: Modification of Hong Kong landscapes by urban development

questions.stem: Figure 1 is a GIS overlay of the urban development map and relief map around Tolo Channel. Roads and settlements form a linear pattern along the valley floor, while adjacent steep slopes have little development. Which explanation is best?
options: Faulting created the valley, and later urban development reshaped its floor into a transport and settlement corridor.
Urban development created the fault valley, so the NE–SW alignment is entirely an artificial landform.
The linear pattern proves that faulting alone determined every settlement location in Hong Kong.
The lack of development on steep slopes shows that relief has no influence on urban distribution.
questions.explanation: Faulting had already shaped the valley before urban development occupied and modified its floor. Faults are locally important, but transport and economic factors influence the final distribution, so they did not determine every settlement location as the main distractor claims.
questions.subtopic_title: Modification of Hong Kong landscapes by urban development

questions.stem: A construction site on a steep Hong Kong slope experiences heavy rain. Which explanation best accounts for the increased risk of a landslide?
options: Heavy rain adds weight and reduces friction, while the steep slope and construction raise shear stress.
Heavy rain reduces stress, the steep slope lowers gravity’s downslope component, and construction adds strength.
Heavy rain removes root binding, while the steep slope and construction both reduce shear strength.
Heavy rain and construction mainly increase resistance, but the steep slope raises the force causing sliding.
questions.explanation: Shear stress is the force tending to cause sliding, while shear strength is resistance to sliding. Heavy rain adds weight and reduces friction, while a steep slope and construction increase shear stress, making failure more likely when stress exceeds strength. Option B incorrectly reverses these effects.
questions.subtopic_title: Slope stability and the factor of safety

questions.stem: Which option correctly identifies one natural and one human factor affecting landslides in Hong Kong and explains each factor’s effect correctly?
options: Heavy rain is natural and adds weight; building construction on a slope is human and adds load.
Heavy rain is natural and removes root binding; slope cutting is human and reduces friction.
A steep slope is natural and reduces friction; construction is human and raises shear strength.
Earthquakes are natural and increase friction; construction is human and removes root binding.
questions.explanation: Heavy rain is a natural trigger that increases slope weight, while building construction is a human activity that adds load and increases shear stress. Option B misassigns the effects: root binding is lost through vegetation removal, and reduced friction is associated with rainwater.
questions.subtopic_title: Slope stability and the factor of safety

questions.stem: During a field trip to Sham Wan, students inspect a steep hillside beside a road. Which observation would provide the clearest evidence of a measure adopted to reduce landslide risk?
options: Drainage channels directing runoff away from the slope
Loose debris deposited at the foot of the slope
Cracks and tilted trees on the hillside
An unpaved footpath crossing the hillside
questions.explanation: Engineered drainage helps prevent water accumulating in the slope, limiting the rise in pore water pressure and maintaining stability. Debris, cracks and tilted trees are signs of instability rather than preventive measures, while a footpath is not itself a slope-protection measure.
questions.subtopic_title: Sham Wan landslide as the official local example

questions.stem: At Yiu Hing Road, hourly rainfall increased from 15 mm to 65 mm before the landslide occurred at 02:36. Which explanation best links rainfall intensity to the slope failure?
options: Infiltration increased pore water pressure, reducing effective stress and slope resistance until failure occurred
Infiltration reduced pore water pressure, increasing effective stress and making the slope more stable
Rainfall had no effect because both landslides failed along pre-existing geological structures
Rainfall of 65 mm per hour was insufficient to trigger a landslide under any conditions
questions.explanation: Higher rainfall intensity allows more water to infiltrate the slope, raising pore water pressure and reducing effective stress and shear resistance. Option B reverses the relationship, while C ignores the rainfall trigger and D contradicts the landslide occurring at that time.
questions.subtopic_title: Sham Wan landslide as the official local example

questions.stem: An earthquake strikes a less developed urban area. Which combination of factors most clearly explains why its vulnerability may be higher?
options: Lower awareness may weaken emergency preparedness, while poorer construction standards increase the risk of collapse.
Higher population density increases exposure, but stronger earthquake-resistant buildings usually prevent collapse.
Daytime population density is lower, so fewer people are likely to be injured or killed.
Greater economic development usually ensures better roads, hospitals and earthquake-resistant building codes.
questions.explanation: Less developed areas may have weaker literacy, awareness and emergency preparedness, while poorer building quality increases the likelihood of collapse. Population density mainly affects exposure, and economic development generally improves building codes and infrastructure rather than making an area more vulnerable.
questions.subtopic_title: Vulnerability of less developed areas and the rationality of living in hazard-prone areas

questions.stem: Which option best represents both an advantage and a disadvantage of living in a hazard-prone area?
options: Fertile volcanic soils support agriculture, while earthquakes and landslides can damage buildings and interrupt essential services.
Attractive landscapes attract tourists, while stronger building codes reduce injuries during earthquakes.
Coastal locations support ports and trade, while effective seismic zoning prevents development in high-risk areas.
Many industries provide employment, while better emergency preparedness reduces deaths after natural hazards.
questions.explanation: Fertile volcanic soils provide an economic benefit, but earthquakes and landslides can cause injury, building and infrastructure damage, and service disruption. Options B, C and D describe risk-reduction measures as advantages, rather than genuine disadvantages of hazard-prone living.
questions.subtopic_title: Vulnerability of less developed areas and the rationality of living in hazard-prone areas

questions.stem: A densely developed Hong Kong shoreline is exposed to wave action and coastal flooding. Which strategy is designed to physically protect buildings and urban land from these hazards?
options: Protect: build seawalls and breakwaters
Reduce: improve drainage and provide early warning
Adapt: elevate buildings and use flexible planning
Avoid: do not build in high-risk areas
questions.explanation: Protection directly reduces coastal hazards by using seawalls and breakwaters, with seawalls especially suitable for protecting urban areas. Adaptation reduces exposure by changing buildings and planning, but it does not physically shield the shoreline from waves and flooding.
questions.subtopic_title: Conflict and the evaluation of management strategies

questions.stem: Which combination best manages river flooding while guiding development and protecting residents in a flood-prone area?
options: Allow flooding in designated areas, apply zoning restrictions and prepare emergency evacuation plans
Allow flooding in designated areas and apply zoning restrictions, but omit evacuation plans
Apply zoning restrictions and prepare evacuation plans, without allowing flooding in designated areas
Elevate buildings and use flexible planning instead of allowing flooding or arranging evacuation
questions.explanation: Effective floodplain management combines allowing flooding in designated areas, restricting development through zoning and preparing emergency evacuation plans. Option C is less effective because zoning and evacuation alone do not provide space for floodwater to spread safely.
questions.subtopic_title: Conflict and the evaluation of management strategies

questions.stem: An irrigated farm in Southern California replaces flood irrigation with a drip network. Which effect best explains this technology's contribution to agricultural productivity?
options: Precise water application allows scarce irrigation water to support higher yields per hectare.
Greater mechanisation eliminates the farm's dependence on seasonal rainfall.
Drip irrigation increases the amount of water diverted from the Colorado River.
Controlled monitoring makes the region's dry summers suitable for rain-fed cropping.
questions.explanation: Drip and sprinkler systems apply scarce water precisely, raising output per hectare and per worker. They do not increase rainfall or Colorado River allocations; Southern California's dry summers still require irrigation.

questions.stem: Which option best describes the complementary economic and political supports sustaining irrigation farming in Southern California?
options: Private capital funds equipment and market facilities, while government provides infrastructure, subsidies, research and regulation.
Private capital replaces government research, while unrestricted river extraction removes the need for regulation.
Government subsidies fund flood irrigation only, while farms avoid cold storage and distant markets.
Research and subsidies raise yields, but transport to distant markets is unnecessary for irrigated crops.
questions.explanation: Capital supports equipment, cold storage, processing and transport, while government provides water infrastructure, subsidies, research and regulation. Option B is wrong because over-allocation of the Colorado River makes effective regulation essential.

questions.stem: Which Hong Kong slope-prevention measure most directly manages the interaction between the hydrosphere and the lithosphere?
options: Drainage systems
Vegetation
Slope inspection
Public education
questions.explanation: Drainage systems directly manage water movement in relation to slope material, linking the hydrosphere and lithosphere. Vegetation also helps stabilise slopes, while inspection and education do not directly alter this interaction.
questions.subtopic_title: The Earth as a system and its internal structure

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how an intrusive (plutonic) igneous rock forms?
options: Magma cools slowly inside Earth, producing large crystals; granite and gabbro are examples.
Magma cools rapidly inside Earth, producing small crystals; granite and gabbro are examples.
Magma cools slowly at Earth's surface, producing large crystals; granite and gabbro are examples.
Magma cools rapidly at Earth's surface, producing large crystals; granite and gabbro are examples.
questions.explanation: Intrusive rocks form when magma cools slowly inside Earth, allowing large crystals to develop; granite and gabbro are examples. Rocks formed at the surface cool rapidly and generally have smaller crystals.
questions.subtopic_title: The Earth as a system and its internal structure

questions.stem: Reclamation projects require large volumes of fill. According to the EP1 distribution of rock types in Hong Kong, which option correctly identifies a major potential source area and its rock type?
options: Volcanic tuff around Tai Mo Shan and Sai Kung
Granite around Ping Chau and the northeastern New Territories
Sedimentary rock around Castle Peak and Kowloon
Metamorphic rock across most of Hong Kong
questions.explanation: Volcanic tuff covers 48% of Hong Kong, with major examples at Tai Mo Shan and Sai Kung. Option B misassigns the examples of sedimentary rock, while option C misassigns granite areas; metamorphic rock covers only a minor area.
questions.subtopic_title: Geological resources: reclamation materials and the Hong Kong International Airport

questions.stem: Hong Kong International Airport is a local reclamation example. If obtaining fill requires extracting material from a distinctive geological formation, which environmental impact should be assessed?
options: Permanent damage to non-renewable geological heritage and disturbance to ecology
Rapid regeneration of the formation after the material is extracted
An automatic increase in the geological uniqueness of the remaining formation
No environmental impact because the material is transferred to reclaimed land
questions.explanation: Geological features do not regenerate once damaged, so extraction may permanently reduce their scientific value and disturb local ecology. Option B is wrong because geological heritage is non-renewable; transferring the material does not remove the extraction impact.
questions.subtopic_title: Geological resources: reclamation materials and the Hong Kong International Airport

questions.stem: In summer, high surface runoff in a steep river valley increases channel flow, causing lateral erosion on the outer bank. Which set of consequences is most likely?
options: A Bank collapse, loss of agricultural land and damage to infrastructure.
B Formation of interlocking spurs and a narrow valley floor.
C Longshore drift and deposition along the shoreline.
D Habitat creation and improvement in water quality.
questions.explanation: Strong channel flow erodes the outer bank, causing bank collapse as a form of mass wasting and potentially damaging farmland and infrastructure. Option D is incorrect because river erosion usually disturbs ecosystems and degrades water quality rather than improving them.
questions.subtopic_title: Mass wasting and ecosystem disturbance as consequences

questions.stem: A Hong Kong river has a large catchment and a steep valley, producing high surface runoff and channel flow in summer. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Outer-bank erosion, possibly causing bank collapse and infrastructure damage
Outer-bank deposition, reducing the risk of damage to nearby infrastructure
Vertical erosion, interlocking spurs and a narrow valley floor in a youthful river stage
Longshore drift, beach deposition and reduced coastal erosion
questions.explanation: The larger catchment, steep valley and summer runoff increase channel flow, promoting outer-bank erosion in the middle to lower course. This may cause bank collapse, loss of agricultural land and infrastructure damage, rather than outer-bank deposition.
questions.subtopic_title: Mass wasting and ecosystem disturbance as consequences

questions.stem: In the semi-arid Sahel, why may adding capital alone to nomadic herding fail to raise agricultural output?
options: Water is the binding constraint, so capital cannot compensate for the lack of reliable water.
Soil fertility is the binding constraint, so fertiliser can solve rainfall and water scarcity.
Skilled labour is the binding constraint, so training can overcome semi-arid environmental limits.
Infrastructure is the binding constraint, so roads and warehouses can guarantee reliable pasture.
questions.explanation: In a semi-arid region, water is the binding production constraint; adding capital without securing reliable water will not raise output. Option B wrongly assumes that improving soil fertility can overcome the more fundamental scarcity of water.

questions.stem: Which explanation best shows how physical, economic, political and socio-cultural factors interact in the Sahel’s nomadic herding system?
options: Low rainfall is the only major constraint; herding practices, poverty and political conditions have little effect on famine risk.
Political instability is the only major constraint; rainfall variability and overgrazing have little effect on agricultural output.
A livestock-based nomadic livelihood is exposed to variable rainfall; overgrazing causes soil erosion, while poverty, weak infrastructure and instability impede recovery.
Commercial farming is inherently safer; nomadic herding contributes little to famine because households can always buy imported food.
questions.explanation: Nomadic herding combines a livestock-based livelihood with exposure to scarce rainfall, while overgrazing can lead to vegetation loss, soil erosion and lower yields. Poverty, limited infrastructure and political instability further weaken coping capacity, so option A wrongly treats rainfall as the only constraint.
